Short case 14 · General Surgery

Neck Swellings

Position and age do most of the work: midline or lateral, and child or adult. Then two signs settle most of the rest, transillumination and movement on swallowing. And one sentence in Bailey & Love 28e should change how you treat a "branchial cyst" in anyone over thirty-five.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1Sort it by position first

PositionSwellings
Midline Thyroglossal cyst · thyroid isthmus swelling · subhyoid bursa · dermoid · enlarged prelaryngeal (Delphian) node · retrosternal extension of goitre
Anterior triangle, upper Branchial cyst · parotid and submandibular swellings · carotid body tumour · lymph nodes · cold abscess
Anterior triangle, lower Thyroid · lymph nodes · laryngocele · pharyngeal pouch
Posterior triangle Cystic hygroma · lymph nodes · cervical rib · lipoma · sternomastoid tumour (in the muscle)
Any site Lymph nodes · cold abscess · lipoma · sebaceous cyst · neurofibroma · lymph cyst

Grouped from SRB ch.5's chapter outline, which lists sternomastoid tumour, cervical rib, branchial cyst and fistula, pharyngeal pouch, laryngocele, cystic hygroma, Ludwig's angina, parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal abscess, tuberculous lymphadenitis, cold abscess and secondaries in neck nodes: SRB ch.5 p.414.

The signs to establish, in B&L's own printed order History; physical signs; size; site; shape; surface; consistency; fixation, deep or superficial; pulsatility; compressibility; transillumination; bruit.B&L 52 · p.805 B&L's opening instruction is that "the clinical signs of size, site, shape, consistency, fixation to skin or deep structures, pulsation, compressibility, transillumination or the presence of a bruit must be established and recorded".B&L 52 · p.805

Pulsatility and bruit are on that list for one reason: the carotid body tumour. Transillumination is on it for another: the cystic hygroma. Do both on every neck swelling and you will not miss either.

2The two signs that settle most cases

Movement on swallowing, and on tongue protrusion
Movement on swallowing means attachment to the larynx or trachea: thyroid, thyroglossal cyst, prelaryngeal node, subhyoid bursa. Movement on protruding the tongue narrows it to a thyroglossal cyst, because the tract runs to the foramen caecum at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior third of the tongue and passes in close continuity with, and sometimes through, the hyoid cartilage.B&L 55 · p.850Das 27 · p.377, p.378
SoGive the patient water first, then ask for the tongue. Two manoeuvres, and the midline differential collapses.
Brilliant transillumination
B&L: "The characteristic that distinguishes it from all other neck swellings is that it is brilliantly transilluminant."B&L 52 · p.805 That is the cystic hygroma, and B&L says it distinguishes it from all other neck swellings, which is as strong a claim as the book makes about any sign.

3Cystic hygroma

What it is
SRB: "a cystic swelling due to sequestration of a portion of the jugular lymph sac from the lymphatic system during the developmental period in utero", with lymphatics failing to communicate with the venous system and abnormal budding of lymphatics; it contains clear lymph with an endothelial lining, and the fluid does not coagulate.SRB 5 · p.424 B&L: the cysts are filled with clear lymph and lined by a single layer of epithelium with a mosaic appearance.B&L 52 · p.805
SynonymCavernous lymphangioma.SRB 5 · p.424
When it presents, and the obstetric consequence
SRB: present at birth and so may cause obstructed labour; occasionally in early infancy.SRB 5 · p.424 B&L: usually in the neonate or early infancy, occasionally at birth and so large as to obstruct labour.B&L 52 · p.805 Both books make the same point, so it is clearly examinable.
The signs
SRB: in the posterior triangle; smooth, soft, fluctuant, partially compressible, brilliantly transilluminant, and not completely reducible; it increases in size during crying.SRB 5 · p.424 B&L: soft and partially compressible, visibly increasing in size when the child coughs or cries, and may be bilateral.B&L 52 · p.805
The worry for the familySRB names it: disfigurement of the child's face, which is more worrying for the parents than the swelling itself.SRB 5 · p.424
Other sites
B&L: besides the neck it may involve the face, submandibular region, tongue and floor of the mouth, and less frequently the cheek, axilla, groin and mediastinum.B&L 52 · p.805 So a cystic hygroma is not only a neck lesion, and tongue or floor-of-mouth involvement is an airway problem.

4Branchial cyst and fistula

Origin
Both books: from the second branchial cleft. SRB's mechanism: "Normally the 2nd, 3rd and 4th clefts disappear to form a smooth neck. Persistent 2nd cleft is called the cervical sinus of His, which eventually gets sequestered to form a branchial cyst." And a second possibility: epithelial infusion within a lymph node, since a branchial cyst contains lymphoid tissue in its wall.SRB 5 · p.419 B&L: from the vestigial remnants of the second branchial cleft, lined by squamous epithelium and containing thick, turbid fluid.B&L 52 · p.805
Where and when it presents
B&L: in the upper neck in early or middle adulthood, at the junction of the upper third and middle third of the sternomastoid at its anterior border; fluctuant, may transilluminate, and often soft in its early stages so that it may be difficult to palpate.B&L 52 · p.805
What the aspirate shows
SRB: the wall shows plenty of lymphoid tissue, it may become infected to form an abscess, and FNAC shows cholesterol crystals; MRI allows finer resolution for preoperative planning.SRB 5 · p.420 Cholesterol crystals in the aspirate is the detail to quote.
The operative anatomy, which is the examiner's next question
B&L: treatment is complete excision, best undertaken when the lesion is quiescent. "It passes superficial to the hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal nerves, but deep to the posterior belly of the digastric. These structures and the spinal accessory nerve must be positively identified to avoid damage."B&L 52 · p.805 Three nerves to name: hypoglossal, glossopharyngeal, spinal accessory.
Branchial fistula
B&L: may be unilateral or bilateral and represents a persistent second branchial cleft. The external orifice is nearly always in the lower third of the neck near the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, the internal orifice on the anterior aspect of the posterior faucial pillar. Where it opens only onto the lateral pharyngeal wall it is a sinus rather than a fistula. The tract is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium, so there may be recurrent mucopurulent discharge onto the neck, and it follows the same path as a branchial cyst and requires complete excision to avoid recurrence.B&L 52 · p.805 SRB adds the acquired version: rupture of a branchial cyst may cause an acquired branchial fistula at the upper third of sternocleidomastoid.SRB 5 · p.420
And the discharge tells youMucus from a neck fistula means branchial.SRB 1 · p.31
A cystic lateral neck swelling in an adult: branchial cyst, or a metastasis? SRB 5 p.420's differential is all benign; B&L 52 p.805 says suspect a necrotic metastatic node over 35
SRB
Gives the differential diagnosis of a branchial cyst as cold abscess, lipoma of the neck, lymph cyst and chronic lymphadenitis; the complications are recurrent infection and rupture producing an acquired fistula; and the treatment is excision.SRB 5 · p.420 Malignancy does not appear in that list.
Bailey & Love 28e
Adds a warning that changes the management: "In patients over 35 years of age, a high index of suspicion for a necrotic metastatic lymph node should exist and" malignancy "should be excluded before excision".B&L 52 · p.805 It also notes that ultrasound is useful precisely for differentiating solid lesions such as malignant lymph nodes from cystic lesions such as a branchial cyst.B&L 52 · p.780
Live and clinically important: the same lump means something entirely different at 20 and at 50, and age is the discriminator.

Answer: "In a young adult at the junction of the upper and middle third of sternomastoid, this is most likely a branchial cyst, and I would confirm with ultrasound and aspiration, which classically shows cholesterol crystals, then excise it when quiescent. But over the age of 35 I would have a high index of suspicion for a necrotic metastatic lymph node and would exclude malignancy before excising anything, because a cystic lateral neck node in an older adult is classically a metastasis from a papillary thyroid carcinoma or an oropharyngeal primary."B&L 52 · p.805SRB 5 · p.420

Why it matters so much: excising a metastatic node as though it were a benign cyst breaches the capsule, seeds the neck and compromises the definitive operation. So the consequence of the error is not a recurrence, it is a worse cancer operation. That is why this one sentence is worth more than the rest of the branchial cyst description.

5Carotid body tumour, and the rule you must not break

SRB's three prohibitions, in seven words "No FNAC, no trucut biopsy, no partial excision."SRB 5 · p.429

Because it is a vascular paraganglioma: needling it bleeds, and partial excision leaves disease on the carotid. It is the one neck swelling where the correct answer to "would you aspirate it?" is an emphatic no, and it is precisely why pulsatility and bruit are on B&L's list of signs to establish in every neck lump.B&L 52 · p.805

Investigation is imaging, and for paragangliomas SRB names a pentetreotide scan using a radiolabelled somatostatin analogue.SRB 5 · p.429 Its differential is carotid artery aneurysm, soft tissue sarcoma, lymph node enlargement, and a vagal neurofibroma, which presents in the carotid triangle as a vertically placed, oval, hard swelling.SRB 5 · p.429

6The rest, in a line each

Thyroglossal cyst
Midline, moves on tongue protrusion as well as swallowing, because the tract runs from the foramen caecum through or close to the hyoid.Das 27 · p.378B&L 55 · p.850 Excision must include the body of the hyoid and the tract, or it recurs.
Sternomastoid tumour
In the muscle itself, in an infant, with torticollis; SRB groups them together.SRB 5 · p.414 Not a tumour but a fibrous contracture.
Cervical rib
Posterior triangle, may be bony hard, and may produce neurovascular symptoms. Test Adson's manoeuvre: the radial pulse disappears when the patient takes a deep breath and turns the head, tightening the scalenes and unmasking the arterial obstruction.SRB 1 · p.166 SRB notes first rib resection can be done thoracoscopically through three ports.SRB 5 · p.419
Pharyngeal pouch and laryngocele
Both lower anterior triangle, both compressible and may gurgle; a laryngocele enlarges on Valsalva and a pharyngeal pouch may empty on pressure. Both are on SRB's list of neck swellings.SRB 5 · p.414 A laryngocele's operative complications include laryngocutaneous fistula and injury to the superior or internal laryngeal nerve, with recurrence.SRB 5 · p.424
Cold abscess
Fluctuant, non-tender, no warmth, no redness, from tuberculous nodes or spine. Aspirate zig-zag, wide bore, non-dependent; drain through a non-dependent incision and close without a drain.SRB 5 · p.433
Ludwig's angina, parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal abscess
On SRB's list,SRB 5 · p.414 and all three are airway emergencies rather than short cases. If you meet one, say so first.
Lymph nodes and secondaries
See the cervical lymphadenopathy case. Remember to report the level, because that is where the primary is.SRB 5 · p.435

7Investigations

Ultrasound first
Because its single best use here is separating solid from cystic, that is a malignant node from a branchial cyst, and because it guides the needle.B&L 52 · p.780
Needle sampling, with two exceptions
Ultrasound-guided FNAC or core biopsy is the standard of care, and core biopsy is preferred for a node because immunohistochemistry needs tissue.B&L 52 · p.781
Do not needleA carotid body tumour or other paraganglioma.SRB 5 · p.429 And think before needling a cystic swelling in an adult over 35, which may be a metastasis needing proper staging.B&L 52 · p.805
MRI
SRB: for a branchial cyst, MRI allows finer resolution during preoperative planning,SRB 5 · p.420 and for a sinus an MR sinusogram is beneficial.SRB 1 · p.33
CT of the thorax
If head and neck malignancy is suspected, to detect distant metastases.B&L 52 · p.780

8Rapid-fire viva

What signs must you establish in any neck lump?

Size, site, shape, surface, consistency, fixation to skin or deep structures, pulsation, compressibility, transillumination and the presence of a bruit, all established and recorded, alongside the history.B&L 52 · p.805 Pulsation and bruit are on that list because of the carotid body tumour, and transillumination because of the cystic hygroma.

Which neck swelling is brilliantly transilluminant?

Cystic hygroma, and Bailey and Love says this is the characteristic that distinguishes it from all other neck swellings.B&L 52 · p.805 It is also soft, partially compressible, not completely reducible, in the posterior triangle, and visibly increases when the child coughs or cries.SRB 5 · p.424

What is a cystic hygroma?

A cystic swelling from sequestration of part of the jugular lymph sac from the lymphatic system in utero, with lymphatics failing to communicate with the venous system and abnormal budding; it contains clear lymph with an endothelial lining, and the fluid does not coagulate. Also called cavernous lymphangioma.SRB 5 · p.424 It is present at birth and may be large enough to obstruct labour, and besides the neck it may involve the face, submandibular region, tongue and floor of mouth, and less often cheek, axilla, groin and mediastinum.B&L 52 · p.805

Where does a branchial cyst arise and present?

From the vestigial remnants of the second branchial cleft; SRB's mechanism is that the persistent second cleft, the cervical sinus of His, becomes sequestered. It is lined by squamous epithelium and contains thick turbid fluid, presents in the upper neck in early or middle adulthood at the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the sternomastoid at its anterior border, and is fluctuant, may transilluminate, and is often soft early so that it is difficult to palpate.B&L 52 · p.805SRB 5 · p.419 FNAC classically shows cholesterol crystals.SRB 5 · p.420

A 50-year-old with a cystic swelling in the upper lateral neck. Would you excise it?

Not before excluding malignancy. Bailey and Love: in patients over 35 a high index of suspicion for a necrotic metastatic lymph node should exist, and malignancy should be excluded before excision.B&L 52 · p.805 A cystic lateral neck node in an older adult is classically a metastasis from a papillary thyroid carcinoma or an oropharyngeal primary. Ultrasound differentiates solid from cystic and guides sampling.B&L 52 · p.780 Excising a metastatic node as though it were a benign cyst breaches the capsule and compromises the definitive cancer operation.

Which nerves are at risk when excising a branchial cyst?

The cyst passes superficial to the hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal nerves but deep to the posterior belly of digastric, and those structures together with the spinal accessory nerve must be positively identified to avoid damage.B&L 52 · p.805 Excision is best done when the lesion is quiescent.

Describe a branchial fistula.

Unilateral or bilateral, representing a persistent second branchial cleft. The external orifice is nearly always in the lower third of the neck near the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid; the internal orifice is on the anterior aspect of the posterior faucial pillar. If it opens only onto the lateral pharyngeal wall it is a sinus rather than a fistula. The tract is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium, so there is recurrent mucopurulent discharge, and it follows the same path as a branchial cyst and needs complete excision to avoid recurrence.B&L 52 · p.805 SRB adds that rupture of a branchial cyst can cause an acquired fistula at the upper third of sternocleidomastoid.SRB 5 · p.420 Mucus discharge from a neck fistula means branchial.SRB 1 · p.31

A pulsatile neck swelling with a bruit. What is it and what must you not do?

A carotid body tumour, a paraganglioma. SRB's rule: no FNAC, no trucut biopsy, no partial excision,SRB 5 · p.429 because it is vascular and partial excision leaves disease on the carotid. Investigate by imaging, with a pentetreotide scan using a radiolabelled somatostatin analogue for paragangliomas. The differential is carotid aneurysm, soft tissue sarcoma, lymph node enlargement, and a vagal neurofibroma, which is a vertically placed, oval, hard swelling in the carotid triangle.

How do you distinguish a midline neck swelling?

Two manoeuvres. Give water: movement on swallowing means attachment to the larynx or trachea, so thyroid, thyroglossal cyst, prelaryngeal node or subhyoid bursa. Then ask the patient to protrude the tongue: movement on tongue protrusion means a thyroglossal cyst, because the tract runs from the foramen caecum at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior third of the tongue, passing in close continuity with and sometimes through the hyoid.Das 27 · p.377, p.378B&L 55 · p.850

Which neck swellings are compressible?

Cystic hygroma, which is partially compressible and increases on crying or coughing;SRB 5 · p.424B&L 52 · p.805 a laryngocele, which enlarges on Valsalva; and a pharyngeal pouch, which may empty on pressure and gurgle. Compressibility is on Bailey and Love's list of signs to establish for exactly this reason.B&L 52 · p.805

A fluctuant, non-tender neck swelling with no warmth or redness.

A cold abscess, from tuberculous lymph nodes or spine. Aspirate zig-zag with a wide-bore needle through a non-dependent area to prevent sinus formation; if formal drainage is needed, use a non-dependent incision and close later without placing a drain.SRB 5 · p.433 Examine the spine, and send material for acid-fast bacilli, culture and cytology.

An infant with a neck swelling and a twisted head.

Sternomastoid tumour with torticollis, which SRB groups together.SRB 5 · p.414 It is not a tumour but a fibrous contracture within the muscle, and the swelling is within the muscle belly, so it becomes less distinct when the muscle is contracted.

How would you investigate a neck swelling of uncertain nature?

Ultrasound first, because it separates solid from cystic, which is the main question, and because it guides the needle; it is also invaluable for salivary pathology.B&L 52 · p.780 Then ultrasound-guided FNAC or core biopsy, preferring core for a node because immunohistochemistry needs tissue.B&L 52 · p.781 MRI for preoperative planning in a branchial cyst.SRB 5 · p.420 CT of the thorax if head and neck malignancy is suspected. And do not needle a pulsatile swelling.

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love, the pharynx, larynx and neck are chapter 52 and the thyroid chapter 55. The one conflict here matters clinically: SRB's differential for a branchial cyst is entirely benign, while the 28th edition warns that over the age of 35 the same swelling should be treated as a possible necrotic metastatic node until malignancy is excluded.
